questions.stem: A 40-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of pain on defecation and hematochezia. He was known to have HIV but had declined previous antiretroviral treatment. A colonoscopy was performed. Investigations: CD4 count 30 cells/μL Colonoscopy: ulcerated mucosa seen; biopsies taken Ulcer histology: amoebic trophozoites with a single nucleus and ingested red blood cells seen. No cysts seen
questions.lead_in: What organism is most likely to be responsible?
questions.explanation: Entamoeba histolytica This is an example of amoebic colitis caused by Entamoeba histolytica. The trophozoites are present in the ulcer and have ingested red blood cells, which is a classic finding in invasive cases. Giardia lamblia is a flagellate protozoan, resides in the small intestine, and does not cause ulcers. Balantidium coli (or Neobalantidium) can cause disease similar to amoebiasis but is a ciliate protozoan. Blastocystis hominis may cause diarrhea but does not ingest red blood cells or cause ulcers.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q31

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man returned from an 8-week trip to India. He had had unprotected oral and anal sex with 2 new male partners while he was traveling. Ten weeks after his return he developed dull pain in the upper abdomen and a high fever. His symptoms had started abruptly. The pain was intense and radiated to the right shoulder. He had associated rigors and profuse sweats. He also noted that his clothes had become loose and that he had a dry cough. He had not had diarrhea. On examination, he was thin and in discomfort. His temperature was 39.9°C. He was markedly tender on palpation of the right upper quadrant and epigastrium, and his liver was palpable three fingerbreadths below the costal margin. Chest examination revealed dull percussion over the right lung base. Investigations: White cell count 15 ×109/L Neutrophils 13.4 ×109/L Eosinophil 0.2 ×109/L Alkaline phosphatase 346 U/L (45–105) CRP 217 mg/L (<10) CXR: raised right hemidiaphragm; small right-sided pleural effusion with loss of the right costophrenic angle Stool microscopy negative Ultrasound liver: round, well-defined hypoechoic mass in the right lobe of the liver; diameter 8 cm Blood cultures and serology are requested.
questions.lead_in: In addition to metronidazole, what therapeutic agent should he receive?
questions.explanation: Paromomycin. This is a case of amebic liver abscess. This is generally managed with a tissue amebicide such as metronidazole and a luminal agent such as paromomycin.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q38

questions.question: A stool test suggests Entamoeba infection.

parts.text: What test should be done next to differentiate Entamoeba histolytica from Entamoeba dispar, and why is that important?

parts_raw.text: What test to do next to differentiate E histolytica vs. E. dispar? Why is that important?

questions.model_answer: a) An E. histolytica–specific test is required because stool O&P microscopy cannot morphologically distinguish E. histolytica from commensal E. dispar and E. moshkovskii: use E. histolytica–specific stool antigen detection (TechLab E. HISTOLYTICA II ELISA, which detects the Gal/GalNAc lectin) or, best, real-time PCR (the gold standard, >95% sensitive/specific on stool). Why it matters: E. dispar (and E. moshkovskii) are non-pathogenic commensals not requiring treatment, whereas E. histolytica is the pathogenic species that causes invasive colitis and liver abscess and should always be treated — so distinguishing them prevents both overtreatment and missed invasive disease.

questions.question: A man from Bogota visiting family in Toronto presents with right upper quadrant pain and a liver abscess on ultrasound. A stool O&P shows the organism pictured (stained blue).
questions.question_raw: Male from Bogota visiting family in Toronto with RUQ pain. There is a liver abscess on ultrasound. He has a stool o/p that shows the picture below (except it was blue)

parts.text: What is the organism?
What is the treatment for the liver abscess, including dose and frequency?
What is one other important treatment, and explain the reasoning for its use?

parts_raw.text: What is the organism?
What is the treatment for the liver abscess, including dose and frequency
What is one other important treatment and explain the reasoning for its use

questions.model_answer: a) Entamoeba histolytica. b) Metronidazole 750 mg PO three times daily x 10 days (drug of choice for amebic liver abscess); tinidazole 2 g PO once daily x 5 days is an alternative. c) A luminal agent — paromomycin 30 mg/kg/day PO in three divided doses x 5–10 days (or diloxanide furoate) — must follow the nitroimidazole because parasites persist in the intestinal lumen in 40–60% of patients treated with a nitroimidazole alone; the luminal agent eradicates residual cysts to cure luminal infection and prevent relapse/transmission. (Do not give the nitroimidazole and paromomycin simultaneously.)

questions.question: A 55-year-old man from Bogota has a liver lesion on imaging; stool shows an Entamoeba trophozoite containing an ingested red blood cell.
questions.question_raw: Q53 - 2023 Day 1 (repeat). 55 guy from Bogota with entamoeba histolytica, liver lesion on imaging and shows E histolytica inside an RBC. (PARASITIC)

parts.text: What is it?
What to treat the liver lesion with, including name, frequency and dose?
Do you need another agent, and why?

parts_raw.text: What is it
What to treat liver lesion with including name, frequency and dose
Do you need another agent and why

questions.model_answer: a) Entamoeba histolytica trophozoite — a protozoan; the ingested erythrocyte (erythrophagocytosis) is the morphologic feature that identifies E. histolytica rather than the morphologically identical commensals E. dispar/E. moshkovskii. b) Metronidazole 750 mg PO three times daily x 10 days (or tinidazole 2 g PO once daily x 5 days). c) Yes — follow with a luminal agent, paromomycin 30 mg/kg/day PO in three divided doses x 5–10 days, because nitroimidazoles fail to clear intraluminal parasites in 40–60% of patients; the luminal agent eradicates residual cysts to cure luminal infection and prevent relapse. Give it after, not concurrently with, the nitroimidazole.

cohort_answer.text:
What is it: Protozoa; unicellular eukaryotic organism. Entamoeba histolytica and Entamoeba dispar are indistinguishable, but if it is in an RBC it is automatically histolytica. Key difference is that Entamoeba histolytica ingests RBCs (Erythrophagocytic).
Treat liver lesion: Metronidazole 750 mg PO TID x 5-10 days (trophozoites) and liver abscess.
Another agent and why: Paromomycin 10mg/kg TID x 5-10 days (for cysts).

questions.question_raw: Travel to India, returns with fever and abdominal pain. US shows 10 cm liver collection

parts.text: Is there any way to differentiate amoebic from pyogenic abscess clinically?

parts_raw.text: A) Any way to differentiate amoebic vs pyogenic clinically?

questions.model_answer: Clinical criteria alone cannot reliably distinguish them — there is near-complete overlap in symptoms. Features favouring amoebic etiology (from one series) are age ≤45, diarrhea, and a solitary right-lobe abscess. A presumptive diagnosis of amoebic abscess rests on positive E. histolytica serology (EIA ~95% sensitive) with a space-occupying lesion on imaging; otherwise aspiration is used to exclude pyogenic abscess.

cohort_answer.text: Not reliable. Need abscess aspiration. Serology

questions.question: A child travelled to South America and is asymptomatic; a stool ova and parasite examination was performed.
questions.question_raw: 27. Child went to South America. Asymptomatic. Had stool O+P.

parts.text: For each of Blastocystis hominis, Entamoeba hartmanni, Trichuris trichiura, and Strongyloides stercoralis: do you treat, and if yes with what drug?
A sibling who also travelled has abdominal pain and a stool O&P showing Entamoeba histolytica/dispar. What one test do you suggest and why?

parts_raw.text: Do you treat and if yes, what drug: Blastocystis hominis / E. hartmanni / Trichuris trichiura / Strongyloides stercoralis
Sibling travelled, had abdo pain and stool O+P shows E. histolytica/dispar. What one test do you suggest and why?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Blastocystis hominis - generally no; treat only if truly symptomatic with no other cause (metronidazole or TMP-SMX). (2) Entamoeba hartmanni - no; non-pathogenic commensal. (3) Trichuris trichiura - yes; albendazole 400 mg or mebendazole x 3-7 days. (4) Strongyloides stercoralis - yes, always treat even if asymptomatic (autoinfection causes lifelong infection and risk of fatal hyperinfection with future immunosuppression); ivermectin 200 ug/kg daily x 2 days. b) Send a stool Entamoeba histolytica-specific antigen test (Gal/GalNAc lectin) or PCR, because microscopy cannot distinguish pathogenic E. histolytica from non-pathogenic E. dispar/E. moshkovskii.
questions.beyond_mandell: Blastocystis, E. hartmanni and E. histolytica/dispar are protozoa outside this chapter; management per IDSA/Mandell protozoa guidance. Strongyloides always-treat rationale and Trichuris therapy grounded in the chapter (pp. 3441, 3437).

b) Husband had self-limited diarrhea illness and is now well. Stool is positive for E. histolytica/dispar. What other test is needed?
c) Test is positive for E. histolytica. What would you treat with?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Strongyloides stercoralis - pathogenic; YES treat regardless of symptoms (lifelong autoinfection, hyperinfection risk); ivermectin 200 ug/kg daily x 2 days (repeat/monitor until larvae undetectable). (2) Entamoeba hartmanni - non-pathogenic commensal; NO treatment. (3) Blastocystis hominis - rarely pathogenic; generally NO treatment; if symptomatic and no other cause, metronidazole or TMP-SMX. (4) Trichuris trichiura - pathogenic (proportional to burden); YES treat; mebendazole (100 mg BID or 500 mg daily) or albendazole 400 mg x 3-7 days, +/- ivermectin. b) An E. histolytica-specific stool antigen (Gal/GalNAc lectin) or PCR, because microscopy cannot distinguish pathogenic E. histolytica from non-pathogenic E. dispar. c) A luminal agent to clear the asymptomatic cyst state: paromomycin 25-35 mg/kg/day divided TID x 7 days (or iodoquinol); if symptomatic invasive disease, first give metronidazole/tinidazole then follow with a luminal agent.
questions.beyond_mandell: Blastocystis, E. hartmanni and E. histolytica/dispar are protozoa outside this chapter; pathogenicity/therapy per IDSA/Mandell protozoa guidance. Strongyloides and Trichuris grounded in the chapter.

cohort_answer.text:
Strongyloides: pathogenic, yes treat (chronic strongy) until larvae no longer detected: Ivermectin 200mcg/kg x2 days 2 weeks apart (cure 94-100%) or Albendazole 400mg BID x3-5d (cure 38-87%). E. hartmanni: commensal, no treatment. Blastocystis hominis: rarely pathogenic, generally no treatment; if treated, Flagyl x10d or Septra x7d. Trichuris: proportional to pathogen amount, yes treat: Mebendazole 100mg PO BID x3d, Albendazole 400mg PO qd x3d, or Ivermectin 200ug/kg PO qd x3d
Antigen test for Gal/GalNAc-lectin to differentiate species; or PCR (microscopy cannot distinguish)
Asymptomatic cyst passer: Paromomycin 25-35mg/kg/day divided TID x7 days ("luminal chaser") OR Iodoquinol 650 TID x21d. If symptomatic diarrhea, would need metronidazole 500 TID x7 days plus paromomycin or iodoquinol after; since asymptomatic might forego that

questions.question_raw: Q9 (2015). Woman recently traveled to rural Cameroon and returned with diarrhea which has now resolved.

parts.text: Stool ova and parasites is performed. For each organism, indicate whether it should be treated and with what: Strongyloides stercoralis; Trichuris trichiura; Dientamoeba fragilis; Entamoeba hartmanni.
Her husband is found to have Entamoeba histolytica/dispar in stool. State one next step and how it would help you.

parts_raw.text: A) Stool O+P is done - indicate which of the following should be treated and with what? Organism | Treatment: Strongyloides stercoralis; Trichuris trichiura; Dientamoeba fragilis; Entamoeba hartmanii
B) Husband found to have entamoeba histolytica/dispar in stool. What is one step you would do next, how would it help you?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Strongyloides stercoralis – YES, treat: ivermectin 200 µg/kg daily × 2 days (cures ~93%); always treat given lifelong autoinfection and hyperinfection risk. (2) Trichuris trichiura – YES, treat: albendazole 400 mg PO × 3–7 days or mebendazole 500 mg daily (or 100 mg BID) × 3–7 days (single-dose therapy has poor cure rates for whipworm). (3) Dientamoeba fragilis – no treatment required in an asymptomatic patient whose diarrhea has resolved. (4) Entamoeba hartmanni – NO, a non-pathogenic ameba, do not treat.
b) Perform a specific test to distinguish E. histolytica from the morphologically identical non-pathogenic E. dispar – a stool antigen (EIA) test or PCR; only E. histolytica is pathogenic and warrants treatment, so this determines whether the husband needs therapy.
questions.beyond_mandell: Ivermectin dosing/cure rate and Trichuris regimens are from this chapter; Dientamoeba fragilis and Entamoeba (hartmanni, histolytica/dispar) are protozoa not covered here – pathogenicity and E. histolytica/dispar differentiation by antigen EIA/PCR are from IDSA/CDC amebiasis guidance. Pre-ivermectin Loa loa screening (endemic in Cameroon) is also outside this chapter.

cohort_answer.text: A) Strongyloides stercoralis - Yes: Ivermectin 200 ug/kg for 2 days or 1 dose repeated 2 weeks after (screen for hypermicrofilaremia with loa loa prior to treatment); Trichuris trichiura - Yes: Mebendazole 500mg PO daily x3 days (superior to albendazole); Dientamoeba fragilis - No; Entamoeba hartmanii - No (non-pathogenic amebae). B) E. histolytica confirmed by trophozoites containing ingested erythrocytes or positive immunoassay AND PCR; PCR differentiates histolytica from dispar - gold standard, 100x more sensitive than antigen assay, up to 100% specific; facilitates early diagnosis and can follow treatment response.

parts.text: Strongyloides – treat, and with what?
Trichuris trichiura – treat, and with what?
Entamoeba hartmanni – treat?
Blastocystis (no symptoms) – treat?
What test differentiates E. histolytica from E. dispar?

parts_raw.text: Strongyloides - treat and with what?
Trichuris trichiura - treat and with what?
Entamoeba hartmanii - treat?
Blastocystis (no symptoms) - treat?
Test to differentiate E. histolytica/dispar

questions.model_answer:
a) Strongyloides: YES – ivermectin 200 µg/kg daily × 2 days (14+ days if disseminated).
b) Trichuris trichiura: YES – albendazole 400 mg × 3–7 days or mebendazole 500 mg daily (or 100 mg BID) × 3–7 days; single-dose therapy has poor cure rates.
c) Entamoeba hartmanni: NO – non-pathogenic ameba.
d) Blastocystis (asymptomatic): NO – do not treat.
e) A stool antigen enzyme immunoassay (EIA) or PCR that specifically detects E. histolytica – microscopy cannot distinguish the pathogenic E. histolytica from the identical non-pathogenic E. dispar; only E. histolytica requires treatment (luminal agent ± tissue amebicide).
questions.beyond_mandell: Entamoeba (hartmanni, histolytica/dispar) and Blastocystis are protozoa not covered in this chapter; their (non-)pathogenicity and the histolytica/dispar antigen-EIA/PCR differentiation are from IDSA/CDC amebiasis guidance. Strongyloides and Trichuris regimens are grounded in this chapter.

cohort_answer.text: Strongyloides: Yes - Ivermectin 1-2 days (non-disseminated). Trichuris trichiura: Yes - Mebendazole x3 days (100mg orally BID x3 days, adults and children). Entamoeba hartmanii: No. Blastocystis (asymptomatic): No. Test: EIA allows E. histolytica differentiation. Treatment if E. histolytica confirmed: asymptomatic = intraluminal agent only (paromomycin x7d); diarrhea/extraintestinal = flagyl 750mg PO TID x7d then intraluminal agent (paromomycin x7d).
